newsitem.title: USA: New England has enough power for summer - NU.
newsitem.headline: New England has enough power for summer - NU.

text.p: Northeast Utilities management expects the company's system and the New England Power Pool will have sufficient capacity to meet New England's peak demand this summer, according to the company's 10K report filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

This is the expectation even if the Millstone nuclear power plants, Maine Yankee and the 300 megawatt Long Island Cable are not operational during the 1997 summer season, so long as the remaining generating units and transmission systems in the New England region operate normally, it said.

If high levels of unplanned outages in New England were to occur, or if any of the NU system's transmission lines used to import power are unavailable, the company and other New England utilities may have to resort to operating procedures to reduce load, the 10K said.
Northeast Utilities said it spend about $60 million to reduce the risk of unplanned outages last year and plans to spend another $47 million this year.
Spokesman Jeffrey R. Kotkin said the $47 million includes $20 million to upgrade transmission facilities and undisclosed lease payments for additional transmission.
The additional capacity is to meet the needs caused by the Millstone outage, the company explained.

The $20 million is part of a $280 million construction program planned for this year, the 10K said. That is up from the $222.8 million spent last year, the $231.4 million spent in 1995, and $259.9 million spent in 1994.
According to the 10K Northeast expects spending to rise again in 1998, to $290 million, then ease to $264 million in 1999, $250 million in 2000 and $260 million in 2001.

The biggest spender will be Connecticut Light & Power Co, which projects spending of $165 million this year. It plans to spend $180 million next year, $164 million in 1999, $163 million in 2000 and $170 million in 2001.

According to the 10K the spending expectations for NU and its subsidiaries are based on a forecast of moderate growth in power sales over the next 10 years in spite of the economic impact of further defense and insurance curtailments.

Forecasting annual growth for the decade of 1.2 percent, NU noted this is significantly below historic rates due to a general slow down of economic growth in the region and, in part, because of programs that manage demand during peak periods.
Without the demand management programs, NU said, the 10-year annual growth rate would be about 1.7 percent.

NU's retail power sales were up 1.6 percent last year after a 0.1 percent decline in 1995, with residential sales increasing two percent and commercial sales up 2.3 percent while industrial sales were essentially flat.

The 10K said weather had a minimal effect in 1996 because the increase in winter heating requirements during an abnormally cold winter was offset by the cool summer's decrease in cooling requirements.
It said Connecticut Light & Power Co power sales rose 1.8 percent last year after a 0.3 percent decline in 1995 and are expected to grow 1.1 percent per year in 1997 through 2006.
Western Massachusetts Electric sales were up 2.7 percent in 1996 after a 0.1 percent decline in 1995 and are projected to grow 0.4 percent annually for 10 years.

Public Service New Hampshire power sales, however, were up only 0.4 percent in 1996, "partly due to the New Hampshire Pilot Program." The program allows selected power users to choose their power suppliers. Sales also increased 0.4 percent in 1995 and are expected to increase 1.7 percent a year through 2006.
